HEADLINE: 'Wealthy selfies' crimp corporate growth
INTRO: Sir Rod Eddington, one of Australia's most experienced directors, has warned that the booming number of self-managed super investors is causing companies to pay out dividends rather than reinvest, amplifying the economic slowdown.
TEXT:
Sir Rod Eddington, one of Australia's most experienced directors, has warned that the booming number of self-managed super investors is causing companies to pay out dividends rather than reinvest, amplifying the economic slowdown.

Speaking after the Australian Bureau of Statistics revealed a record fall in capital expenditure in 2015-2016, the prominent businessman said the lack of confidence was the major reason for corporate Australia's spending strike. But he agreed that the rising number of self-managed super funds (SMSFs) was playing a more influential role in capital markets.

"There are lots of reasons why boards are being cautious on investment plans," Sir Rod told AFR Weekend. "The issue of dividend streams is one of them."

Friday saw fresh evidence of the lack of investment, with Reserve Bank of Australia figures showing bank lending grew in April at the weakest pace in 17 months.

Lending grew by just 0.3 per cent in the month, led by a complete loss of momentum on business lending, which was unchanged from the previous month.

April was the first time business lending failed to grow in any month in more than two years, and adds to Thursday's bleak official figures that showed spending by companies on new equipment, machinery and buildings fell by the most since the global financial crisis.

While companies point to a lack of confidence as the chief cause of the problem, corporate boards are also finding themselves under increased pressure to keep their share prices afloat by paying ever-increasing dividends. There are now just over one million self-managed superannuation funds in Australia, controlling almost $600 billion. Such investors typically prefer high dividend yielding stocks to provide retirement income.

Credit Suisse on Friday calculated SMSFs now own 16 per cent of the Australian share market.

"Our aging, wealthy Selfies underpin demand for Aussie dividends, especially those which come with franking," said Hasan Tevfik, an analyst at Credit Suisse.

He said Australian companies will continue to want to "keep them happy", but they may have to continue to cut capital spending investment to do that.

"Selfies don't seem to care," Mr Tevfik said.

Saul Eslake, chief economist at Bank of America Merrill Lynch, believes company decision-making is being driven by what are essentially three negative factors.

"They're genuinely struggling to see where the increased demand for their products will come from, and that's a global phenomenon," he said.

"Point two, although risk-free rates on return have come down an awful lot, companies would probably argue that the risk premium has gone up - not only is there uncertainty about the economic outlook, there's geopolitical uncertainty.

"Point three, specifically in Australia, there clearly has been a deterioration in business confidence, which is probably a product of people's assessment of the political environment."

Sir Rod, chairman of J.P. Morgan Australasia and a former chief executive of British Airways, said whether boards spent more on capital projects or paid out dividends was a complex issue. There was plenty of cash sitting inside Australian companies, he said. "At a time of uncertainty, directors don't want to put that at risk."

Other corporate directors pointed to a difficult balancing act where a lack of business opportunities make paying out dividends a better option - even the lack of investment could crimp future growth.

Rod Walker, chairman of vacuum cleaner retailer Godfreys and clothing retailer PAS Group, says there is always a balance that needs to be found in allocating capital.

"You need the opportunity to be there and if it's not, you can't invest in it."

Ross Barker, who oversees $6.5 billion for Australian Foundation Investment Company, said companies would invest more in their own businesses if the likely returns are forecast to exceed their cost of capital. If it doesn't, they won't.

HEADLINE: OFFSIDE
INTRO: FIFA After years of courting the most powerful man in football, Australia's top soccer boss has cut Sepp Blatter loose. What's Frank Lowy up to, asks John Stensholt.
TEXT:
FIFA After years of courting the most powerful man in football, Australia's top soccer boss has cut Sepp Blatter loose. What's Frank Lowy up to, asks John Stensholt.

Frank Lowy didn't muck around when he became chairman of Football Federation Australia in 2003.

Australia was a backwater on the world football scene, but the Westfield supremo was determined to make his mark - by going straight to the top.

Sepp Blatter, president of world governing body FIFA, was the man Lowy wanted to reach. And given the businessman's extensive connections it turned out he could. Lowy got on the phone to his long-time mate John Coates, the Australian Olympics boss and a mover and shaker at the International Olympics Committee, of which Blatter is also a member.

Coates arranged a lunch between the two sporting heavyweights in Geneva later that year and the pair hit it off. Lowy, a post-war migrant who grew up watching and loving football, instantly connected with the Swiss football boss, and their friendship blossomed.

So much so that when Lowy docked his luxury boat Ilona in Athens for the 2004 Olympics he invited Blatter and other FIFA dignitaries to enjoy first class food and drinks on board.

It seemed that all of a sudden Australia, via the powerful and persuasive figure of Lowy, was a player on the football scene.

Not known for resting on his laurels, Lowy worked on his relationships with the powerful figures in world football and things only got better for the soccer minnow.

He even convinced football's elite to travel to Sydney for the FIFA congress in 2008, during which Blatter actively encouraged the billionaire to lead a bid by Australia for the greatest prize of them all, hosting rights for the World Cup in 2022.

That disastrous bid is the dark cloud Lowy seemingly will never be able to escape. Qatar won the hosting rights in a vote 2010 - and Australia, to Lowy's eternal embarrassment, received one paltry vote.

Lowy was pragmatic enough to vote for Blatter again in 2011 when the FIFA president stood successfully for re-election.

But in a startling turn of events this week, Lowy turned against his football associate.

The stunning arrests of several FIFA executives on alleged corruption charges prompted Lowy and the FFA to back Blatter's challenger for this year's election (to be held overnight Friday, Australian time), Prince Ali bin Al-Hussein of Jordan.

What then prompted the Football Federation Australia chairman to finally cut Blatter loose?

It probably comes down to simple self-interest. In the waning days of his stewardship as chairman of FFA, Lowy has presided, in his own inimitable style, over more than a decade of huge growth for football in Australia.

He wants to go down in history as the man who changed the beautiful game in Australia forever. His hard work recognised and his legacy as saviour cemented.

After the best part of a decade of trying work within the system Lowy finally found his voice.

On Thursday evening Lowy, who was in Zurich for the FIFA conference, announced: "FFA believes that profound change within FIFA is needed as soon as possible to address issues of governance and transparency."

But why has he moved to fight the system which is lauded so much?

Does he and the FFA really want to bring about change in world football?

Or has Lowy sniffed the breeze and figured Blatter was going to be voted out and the weight of numbers was with Prince Ali anyway? Or that at the very least voting for the Jordanian would not bring with it any reprisals even if Blatter is to hang on and win another four years in charge of the world's most popular sport?

Previous history would suggest Lowy is being calculated. No matter what he has done for football in Australia - and his achievements are considerable - Australia's bid for the 2022 World Cup, incredibly awarded to Qatar, but one that engulfed Australia in controversy, has never gone away and probably never will.

The move to distance FFA from the corruption charges and join in the fight to bring about change to the governance of world football could certainly been seen as a plan to save face as controversy continues to rage about that World Cup bid.

Lowy's style for the past decade has been to work inside FIFA's tent, diplomatically working the backrooms, meeting and trying to curry favour with the cast of characters that run the sport - many of whom now face corruption charges or have already been thrown out.

It has worked. Mostly.

It has gained Australia great success but also, in the case of the ill-fated World Cup bid, great embarrassment.

It certainly worked well for Lowy in his courting of Blatter, particularly during the World Cup bid.

But more recently there has been visible tension between the two. It was palpable when Blatter came to Australia in January for the Asian Cup.

And it surfaced again when Lowy agreed to Blatter's recommendation that FFA hire controversial consultant Peter Hargitay. Together with fellow consultants Andreas Abold and Fedor Radmann, Hargitay was meant to work the corridors of FIFA power and convince voters Australia was the best choice to host 2022.

Paying the trio cost more than $12 million, out of the $46 million the Australian federal government provided in funding for the bid.

The strategies the consultants recommended were aggressive, including currying as much favour as possible with countries from where the 24 voters came from. Australia played Paraguay, where one member of the FIFA executive committee hailed from, in a lucrative friendly. Money was also provided for a Trinidad and Tobago youth team to travel to a tournament in Europe.

Trinidad is the country of Jack Warner, the then head of the Confederation of North, Central American and Caribbean Association Football (CONCACAF). When asked what legacy program Australia could provide funding for, FFA was told funding for stadium upgrade in Trinidad and Tobago would be ideal.

A payment of about $500,000 was sent through, but, disastrously for the FFA, it ended up in Warner's personal bank account. Australian football authorities insist it was by accident and wasn't a bribe. Warner later resigned from his long-held FIFA roles and was among the those arrested at the behest of FBI this week.

Also, co-operating with the FBI has been former US soccer boss Chuck Blazer. He has turned informant after a long career deep inside the FIFA tent.

The New York Daily News last year reported that Lowy was among several football identities Blazer invited to meet with him during the 2012 Olympics.

Then there was Bin Hamman. Lowy and then FFA chief executive John O'Neill worked closely with Bin Hamman, then head of the Asian Football Confederation, to smooth the path for Australia to join the AFC from Oceania.

Lowy described the Qatari Bin Hamman as a "brother" and worked hard to convince him to get Asia to back Australia's 2022 World Cup bid. But Bin Hamman, according to length accusations documented by the Sunday Times was instead secretly working to allegedly bribe voters to cast in favour of his home country. He was later banned by FIFA for life and the Qatar organisers said Bin Hamman had worked without their knowledge.

Passionately, stubbornly, belligerently and with plenty of force, Lowy has overseen an increasingly popular national A-League and success for the Socceroos national team, including three consecutive World Cup qualifications and the winning of the Asian Cup in January.

Add to that was a masterstroke by Lowy to shift the FFA away from Oceania region to Asia. It is one that will ensure he will be regarded as the most influential person in Australian football history. The 84-year-old has only months left as FFA chairman, being required by the organisation's constitution to step down later this year from the position he has held since 2003. He hopes his son Stephen will follow in his footsteps and become the next chairman.

Four-and-a-half years have passed since Lowy, FFA officials, then Sports Minister Mark Arbib and a cast of celebrities that included glamour model Elle McPherson gathered in Zurich to hopefully hear the news Australia had won the race to host the 2022 World Cup.

Perhaps Lowy, before he steps down from FFA, can help engineer real change at FIFA. Change that would rid the world game of the long shadow of corruption, cash payments in brown paper bags and trail of money ziz-zagging the world.

It could be part of a heroic effort that topples Blatter and sets FIFA on the path towards proper corporate governance and stricter financial controls, and build a solid base for the game to flourish.

And maybe it would make people forget about Australia trying to play the same game as part of the World Cup bid. Perhaps.

MR SOCCER

2003 Frank Lowy becomes chairman of Football Federation Australia

2005 A-League launched and  Australia strikes agreement to join Asian Football Confederation

2006 Australia plays in World Cup for first time in 32 years

2010 Australia loses bid for 2022  World Cup

2015 Australia hosts and wins Asian Cup

HEADLINE: Howes signed off on controversial cleaners' deal
INTRO: An executive of a cleaning company that struck a deal with the Australian Workers' Union, trading away millions of dollars in workers' pay, admitted the agreement wouldn't have passed the workplace regulator.
TEXT:
An executive of a cleaning company that struck a deal with the Australian Workers' Union, trading away millions of dollars in workers' pay, admitted the agreement wouldn't have passed the workplace regulator.

It has been alleged the AWU agreed to trade away some of the nation's lowest-paid workers' penalty rates in return for $25,000 a year in a deal that saved Cleanevent, a subsidiary of Spotless, $2 million.

Giving evidence on Friday, former Cleanevent human resources manager Michael Robinson told the hearing he feared the memorandum of understanding (MOU) would be "quashed" by the Fair Work Commission as it would have failed the "better off overall test. At the time, I was hopeful this agreement would be in place [for] as long as possible," Mr Robinson said. "I believe [it] had benefits for the company and the AWU."

Mr Robinson believed from discussions with the Victorian branch of the AWU that the MOU would have had to be passed through the national office.

Documents lodged with the royal commission into trade unions reveal former union boss Paul Howes signed off on the 2010 MOU between Cleanevent and the union.

The deal was negotiated by Cesar Melhem and a former state organiser, John-Paul Blandthorn, now an adviser to Victorian Premier Daniel Andrews.

AWU sources said on Friday that, under its rules, agreements covering more than one branch are negotiated by the branches and signed off by the national secretary once the branches declare they meet standards required by the union.

It has been alleged the 2010 deal saw the company maintain pay rates from the 2006 bargaining agreement and, in return, the union receive $25,000 a year for three years and a list of names from the company of its casual workforce, without the employees' knowledge, which were entered into the union's membership roll.

It is believed the deal saved the company an estimated $2 million a year in penalty rates.

HEADLINE: Investor surge defies home loan limit
INTRO: The surge in lending to property investors continued in April as the value of home loans held by landlords once again grew by more than the banking regulator's cap of 10 per cent a year.
TEXT:
The surge in lending to property investors continued in April as the value of home loans held by landlords once again grew by more than the banking regulator's cap of 10 per cent a year.

But in a potential sign that regulators' heightened scrutiny of banks may be having some impact, the annual rate of housing investor credit growth has at least levelled off, rather than accelerating as it did in previous months.

Reserve Bank figures on Friday showed housing investor credit expanded by 10.4 per cent in the year to April, equalling a seven-year high from the previous month, and exceeding the Australian Prudential Regulation Authority's (APRA) cap of 10 per cent a year, announced in December.

National Australia Bank, ANZ Bank, and Westpac all expanded their investor home loan books by more than 10 per cent over the period, separate figures from APRA showed.

The signs of ongoing strength in investor lending come after banks in recent weeks taking action to curb investor lending, including cutting discounts for investors, and requiring larger deposits from some borrowers.

JP Morgan economist Stephen Walters said he believed APRA would need to adopt a tougher approach to slow lending, including threatening banks with tougher capital rules.

"Our argument is that they are probably going to need more than moral suasion, because on that evidence it's not enough," Mr Walters said.

All big banks have now cut discounts for housing investor borrowers, and Macquarie Group told brokers of further changes to its credit policies this week, including maximum loan-to-valuation ratios (LVR) for some products.

A note from Macquarie said it would introduce a maximum LVR of 80 per cent for new loans where the main purpose of the loan was for owner-occupied housing, and any portion of the loan was interest-only. Several other types of loans, including those for investment, would have a 90 per cent LVR cap, the note said. The bank also announced changes to its pricing structure for variable-rate loans, with the lowest rates offered on owner-occupier products where the borrower paid back principal and interest.

Beyond housing, the RBA figures showed credit growth across the whole economy slowed to 0.3 per cent in April, from 0.5 per cent in March. Personal credit, business credit and lending to owner-occupiers all slowed.

The slowdown in business borrowing is likely to reflect the low level of confidence in corporate Australia, which was underlined in numbers that this week pointed to a 25 per cent plunge in capital expenditure in 2015-16.

HEADLINE: Inheritance bonanza funded by super
INTRO: This year an estimated $8.5 billion will be bequeathed by the estates of Australians who die before using up their retirement savings, according to superannuation advisory firm Rice Warner.
TEXT:
This year an estimated $8.5 billion will be bequeathed by the estates of Australians who die before using up their retirement savings, according to superannuation advisory firm Rice Warner.

It's a figure that will no doubt interest the federal government, which wants people to spend their superannuation rather than trying to keep it for inheritance purposes.

Social Services Minister Scott Morrison, in defending pension changes contained in the budget, has cited departmental figures that show some retirees receiving a part-pension from the government are able to maintain - and even grow - their assets in the five years before their deaths.

"It is not unreasonable for people who have benefited from tax concessions to build up sizeable superannuation balances, to then be expected to draw down on those balances in retirement, rather than draw on a taxpayer funded pension," he has said.

So how much money does the average superannuant still have as they approach the end? According to Treasury, most still have around half of their super balances when they reach average life expectancy, which in 2014 was 85 for women and 83 for men.

Rice Warner consultant Nathan Bonarius calculates that at present the average Australian retiree reaches 80 with assets worth $110,000. In 15 years, the average at 80 will be $300,000.

In aggregate, death benefits flowing from account-based pensions will be $8.5 billion in 2014-15, he says.

Getting people to run down their super balances might sound simple, but nobody knows how much money they will need because they don't know how long they will live. Experts say many retirees live more frugally than necessary but others run out of super and end up on the pension in their latter years. The fact that Australia is moving closer to a user-pays aged care system only adds to people's anxiety.

"You wouldn't aim to spend all of your money by life expectancy, and pensioners are quite rational to behave that way," Bonarius says.

"The issue is people who effectively use superannuation as a tax-exempt savings vehicle and the average Australian doesn't do that."

Indeed, critics say the government's pension changes will hurt middle Australia while leaving the wealthiest unscathed.

Asset test changes mean the point at which a retiree's pension is affected will be increased to $375,000 for couples who own their home. A second change is an increase in the so-called taper rate from $1.50 to $3.

"This pension debate is affecting middle Australia, not higher income Australia, because higher income Australia doesn't get any age pension," says Mercer consultant David Knox, who thinks the government should consider a $2 taper rate. "I think there is validity in the argument to say if we're going to tighten up the age pension, you also have to review the taxes on super."

The government, however, has promised not to touch superannuation and dumped a planned review into retirement incomes.

Nevertheless, a range of submissions to the government's tax review, due on Monday, will likely call for changes to tax concessions for superannuation, which are seen to favour the rich.

PwC partner Catherine Nance, convener of the Institute of Actuaries retirement income taskforce, says not all tax concessions go to the rich, and when the age pension is taken into account, concessions are fairly evenly distributed across income bands. For example, 67 per cent of concessions go to those earning $37,000 to $180,000, she says. Nevertheless, important changes were required to make the system fairer. A lifetime pension-phase cap of $2.5 million could be applied, Ms Nance said.

HEADLINE: Make drivers pay for traffic congestion
INTRO: Here is something I'll bet you didn't need Infrastructure Australia to tell you: the Sydney-Newcastle-Wollongong conurbation has the most expensively congested roads in Australia.
TEXT:
Here is something I'll bet you didn't need Infrastructure Australia to tell you: the Sydney-Newcastle-Wollongong conurbation has the most expensively congested roads in Australia.

Annual congestion costs in the three major NSW cities are almost twice those of Melbourne-Geelong and three times those of Brisbane-Gold Coast-Sunshine Coast.

Indeed, traffic congestion across Australia's capital cities imposes a serious cost on workers and the road freight industry, and therefore the national economy.

And here is something else you might have guessed without any official help: some of the biggest, most expensive traffic jams are on the very same roads on which you were ensnarled years ago.

The often heavily politicised distribution of road spending, you might suspect, has not been as efficient as it could have been.

By week's end, no doubt, you would have been rotated by the evening television news through the usual cast of politicians, urban planners and public transport activists with their familiar and apparently ineffective solutions: motorways, transit lanes, light rail, car pooling, and so on.

There is a "solution", but it is not simple or costless. Nor can we expect our politicians to attempt it without strong support from the public.

It begins with increasing the incentives for governments to allocate the money for transport infrastructure properly.

A key part of the solution, the economists tell us, is a proper system of congestion pricing or road tolls.

Roads are overused for the same reason the old English commons were over-grazed and the oceans are over-fished: because access is free and there is no incentive for any one of us to take account of the cost we impose on the other users.

The solution in all cases is to ration the use of the limited resource, which we can do most efficiently by charging a price at least equal to the cost imposed by the user.

That's easier said than it is politically done, however.

Road tolls on private roads and tunnels might already be a familiar part of the landscape, but those tolls are quite different from the congestion charges we now need.

In nearly all cases, the existing tolls are on new roads. The new road charges we need to "solve" the congestion problem would apply to the existing, inadequate roads.

When you or I drive into an already congested road, we add to the congestion that causes the traffic to move more slowly. But while we might take account of the cost to ourselves - in time and petrol - of using the congested road, we don't take account of the additional cost we are imposing on everyone else.

That additional cost to each of the other motorists might be very small but, because there are a lot of them, the toll could be substantial.

So what can we hope to achieve with all this? Certainly not the elimination of traffic congestion: something like a quarter of congestion is said to be the result of breakdowns, accidents, bad weather and other unexpected events. We wouldn't even eliminate the "recurring" congestion that occurs predictably as the road approaches full capacity.

No one would be willing to pay a toll large enough to turn the morning peak hour on Sydney's Parramatta Road into a pleasant Sunday spin, and it would be inefficient. However, we would achieve something important.

Everyone would be required to cover the cost of additional congestion they impose on the system.

For some people, that would be enough incentive to get up earlier or travel later or find some other alternative to peak-hour motoring. And even a relatively small reduction in peak-hour traffic can make a significant difference to the traffic flow.

In the process, it could also put off the day when the taxpayers will have to invest in a wider road.

The toll-paying motorists might be worse off (the toll almost certainly would exceed the value of the time saved), but the community as a whole would be better off because of the delay in the need for new investment.

Indeed, even where there was very little improvement in the congestion and traffic flow, because motorists were unable to change their travel patterns, the congestion charge could play a useful role.

The money piling up in the government's coffers would be a signal that additional investment was warranted.

Charging motorists for congestion surely would increase the pressure on governments to spend money on reducing congestion.

That should lead to an improvement in the allocation of resources.

In NSW, for example, the money being lavished on the North West rail link might have been spent on fixing the roads had there been more intense pressure from motorists and the road freight industry.
